articleTitle: Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations for Recrystallization Process of Discrete Amorphous Regions in C3 H5-Molecular-Ion-Implanted Silicon Substrate Surface
abstract: The proximity gettering technique using ion-implantation-induced defects is attracting considerable attention to prevent leakage current which caused by contaminated transition metallic impurity in active regions of sensitive device such as complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) image sensors. Especially, defects formed by monomer carbon implantation are known to perform high gettering capability for transition metallic impurities contaminated in device active regions [1, 2]. On the other hand, we have developed C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted epitaxial silicon (Si) wafers to provide additional advantageous features for improving CMOS image sensors performance [3–9]. This novel concept proximity gettering Si wafers are manufactured by implanting C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ions into a Czochralski (CZ)-grown Si substrate and then epitaxial Si layer growth on implanted Si substrate surface. The C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ion projection ranges are located underneath device active regions in epitaxial Si layer and function well as powerful gettering sink for transition metallic impurities. This C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ion projection ranges also have barrier effect against oxygen diffusing out from the CZ-grown Si substrate to the device active regions in epitaxial Si layer. In addition, in device fabrication process, hydrogen trapped in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ion projection ranges are diffused out and passivate dangling bonds at SiO<inf>2</inf>/Si interface in device structure and prevent leakage current. Moreover, in order to satisfy severe electrical characteristics of advanced CMOS image sensors, it is necessary to enhance the gettering capability for transition metallic impurities and the passivation effect own to hydrogen trapped in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ion projection ranges. One simple solution to enhance gettering capability and hydrogen passivation effect is high-dose implantation of C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ions. High-dose implantation of C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ions increases the density of defects consisting of carbon and interstitial Si atoms, which served as gettering sink [3]. Additionally, hydrogen trapped in the projection range also increase linearly with high-dose implantation condition of C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ions [6]. However, in high-dose C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ion implantation condition, it is reported that numerous discrete amorphous regions are formed in Si substrate surface due to overlapping of each molecular ion implantation damage [7]. Therefore, subsequent thermal annealing treatment must be applied to recrystallize discrete amorphous regions in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted Si substrate surface prior to epitaxial Si layer growth [8, 9]. In order to achieve crystal perfection of Si substrate surface by optimizing thermal annealing treatment condition, it is necessary to clarify recrystallization behavior of C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted Si substrate surface. However, recrystallization process of discrete amorphous regions in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted Si substrate surface is still not revealed. In addition, in terms of crystallinity of Si substrate surface after thermal annealing treatment, understanding of recrystallization dimension is crucial to anticipate which type of defect formation after recrystallization. In previous study, two-dimensional recrystallization of amorphous regions generate crystalline boundaries and corner defects are occasionally remained after three-dimensional recrystallization of amorphous regions [10–13]. Although, it is difficult to observe detailed recrystallization behavior of nanometer-scale discrete amorphous regions in Si substrate surface during several seconds thermal annealing treatment experimentally using conventional cross-sectional or plan-view transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Therefore, in this study, we investigate the recrystallization process of discrete amorphous regions in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted Si substrate surface by Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD) process simulator using Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) approach [14]. Firstly, we calculate distribution and concentration of vacancy and interstitial Si atom induced by high-dose C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf> molecular ion implantation into Si substrate using Monte Carlo (MC) ion implantation simulations [15]. Then, from the distribution and concentration of vacancy and interstitial Si atom, amorphous regions of C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted Si substrate are obtained and compare with the cross-sectional TEM images. Furthermore, using KMC simulations, we calculate recrystallization via solid phase epitaxial growth (SPEG) from the amorphous/crystalline interface of each discrete amorphous regions in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecula-ion-implanted Si substrate surface and compare with the plan-view TEM images when subsequent thermal annealing treatment is applied. After confirmation of correspondence between simulated models and experimental observations, we analysis the detailed recrystallization process of discrete amorphous regions in C<inf>3</inf> H<inf>5</inf>-molecular-ion-implanted Si substrate surface and discuss these mechanism.

articleTitle: Innovative Annealing Technology for Thermally Stable Ni(GeSn) Alloys
abstract: GeSn alloys are very promising materials for Si-based photonics and CMOS technologies. Performant contacts are definitely needed to make the most of innovative Mid Infra-Red (MIR) GeSn-based devices such as Light Emitting Devices, electrically pumped lasers, photo-detectors and so on. The most reported metallization scheme on GeSn is based on Ni. Ni has indeed the advantage of forming a Ni(GeSn) alloy at relatively low temperature that exhibits low resistivity and contact resistance. On the other hand, the main drawback of the Ni(GeSn) alloy is its poor thermal stability because of 2 phenomena: Ni(GeSn) agglomeration and Sn segregation. Technological alternatives have thus been evaluated to enhance the thermal stability of the Ni / GeSn system. As for instance, the use of pre-amorphization by implantation (PAI) prior to metallization and the addition of alloying elements, such as Pt and Co, have been reported in Ni-based metallization [1–3].

articleTitle: Improving FinFET Junctions and Contacts via Laser Annealing
abstract: Semiconductor industry transitions from the era of planar FETs to the era of three-dimensional (3D) transistors greatly improving performance per footprint. In planar FETs, the gate width W<inf>G</inf>, the lateral source/drain (S/D) size, and the metallic contact width W<inf>C</inf> are all equal to the transistor width W. FinFETs feature a 3D channel geometry where the gate perimeter W<inf>G</inf> per fin or, equivalently, the effective channel width W<inf>eff</inf> is significantly larger than the fin pitch P that defines the S/D and metallic contact width per fin (Fig. 1). Large W<inf>eff</inf> reduces the channel resistance but small P increases the parasitic external resistance R<inf>EXT</inf> making it a performance limiting factor. Innovative processes and new materials are required for reducing components of R<inf>EXT</inf> thereby realizing FinFET performance advantage. This work explores millisecond and nanosecond laser annealing techniques for reducing FinFET R<inf>EXT</inf> focusing on source/drain and contact resistances. Transistor-level specific contact resistivity in sub 10<sup>-9</sup> Ω-cm<sup>2</sup> range has been achieved for both nFETs and pFETs with corresponding improvements in R<inf>EXT</inf> and switching currents.

articleTitle: Nanosheet-based Device Architectures with Front/Backside Connectivity: Opportunities for S/D Engineering to Enable Advanced CMOS Logic Scaling
abstract: We report on nanosheet-based FETs as key enablers for the continuation of the CMOS logic scaling roadmap beyond finFETs. Their source/drain (S/D) definition is an important differentiator, done via inner spacers and S/D epi growth co-integration, for single or, in case of 3D stacked structures such as CFET, multiple transistor vertical levels. Different S/D-induced channel strain scenarios motivate exploration of alternative S/D epi processes and materials, particularly for NMOS stacked on top of PMOS in CFET. In parallel, for enhanced performance and higher cells scalability, power wiring can be moved to the wafer’s backside (BS). In this work, taking advantage of such configuration, we will also discuss several possible options for further contact resistance (R<inf>contact</inf>) reduction at the transistor’s source, thus engineering devices from both the wafer’s frontside (FS) and its BS.

articleTitle: Temporary and spatially resolved luminescence studies of p-GaN segments fabricated by vacancy-guided redistribution of Mg using sequential ion implantation of Mg and N
abstract: For realizing high-performance GaN power-switching devices, establishing an ion-implantation (I/I) technique to control conductivity type and conductivity in designated segments of GaN is an urgent issue. However, fabricating p-type GaN by Mg doping, especially p-GaN:Mg formation by I/I, has long been a tough job. The difficulty in Mg I/I arises from the fact that high concentration (>10<sup>19</sup> cm<sup>-3</sup>) divacancies comprising a Ga vacancy (V<inf>Ga</inf>) and a nitrogen vacancy (V<inf>N</inf>), namely V<inf>Ga</inf> V<inf>N</inf>, or trivacancies [V<inf>Ga</inf>(V<inf>N</inf>)<inf>2</inf>] are introduced by Mg I/I and they agglomerate into (V<inf>Ga</inf> V<inf>N</inf>)<inf>3</inf> clusters by a post-implantation annealing (PIA) [1]. Because such vacancy complexes have been assigned as deleterious nonradiative recombination centers (NRCs) [2], gross amount of vacancies should be minimized and therefore suppressing gross I/I-induced damage is indispensable.

articleTitle: The Evolution of Bonding from Packaging to the Front End
abstract: Wafer processing and assembly and packaging have been distinct, separate areas of semiconductor processing since the very beginning of the semiconductor era. However, with device scaling reaching fundamental limits, advanced packaging incorporating stacking with traditional FEOL technologies (such as CMP) and scaled packaging technologies (such as bonding, thinning, TxV) is now in the forefront for achieving higher bandwidth and density. This presentation focuses on bonding, beginning with a short overview of different bonding technologies. It will then transition to a discussion of fusion and hybrid bonding and their applications in the semiconductor industry. Hybrid bonding, with its multiple benefits of scalability, reliability, SI/PI and across stack thermal conductivity, is rapidly emerging as a key enabler of heterogenous integration, so the focus will then shift to an in-depth discussion of fusion and hybrid bonding technology, with applications ranging from CMOS image sensors to high performance computing to stacked FET [1].

articleTitle: Sheet Resistance Reduction of Sputtered WS2 Film by Cl2 Plasma Treatment for Thermoelectric Devices
abstract: Reduction of electric power consumption is urgently required, therefore thermoelectric devices are attracting attention as a power regeneration method. The thermoelectric devices are environmentally friendly, because wasted heats are directly converted into electricity with the Seebeck effect. A Bi<inf>2</inf> Te<inf>3</inf> is currently a major thermoelectric material which has the Seebeck coefficient of about -7.56×10 [μV/K] [1] at room temperature, however higher thermoelectric performance is required for future highly efficient usage. Therefore, we selected a tungsten disulfide (WS<inf>2</inf>) film, which is a kind of TMDC (Transition Metal Di-Chalcogenide) material with atomic 2D structure [2] [3] [4]. The WS<inf>2</inf> film has been reported to have the Seebeck coefficient of about 1.17×10<sup>3</sup> [μV/K] [5] and is expected to be a new flexible semiconductor material. However, to maximize thermoelectric performance, the carrier density must be controlled as about 5 × 10<sup>19</sup> [cm<sup>-3</sup>] [6].

articleTitle: Exploring Next-Generation GaN Power Devices with Ferroelectric Charge Trap Gate Stack Technology for Normally-OFF Operations
abstract: In light of the escalating global energy consumption and the concomitant demand for sustainable energy, optimizing energy efficiency has emerged as a crucial goal for advancing next-generation power-switching devices applications. As the quest for high-power density, compactness, and cost-effectiveness of devices persists in future power electronics applications, conventional Si-based devices are progressively encountering their physical boundaries. Considerable research and resources have been directed towards integrating renewable resources into electrical power conversion systems with optimal efficiency. Consequently, the replacement of traditional power systems with wide-bandgap semiconductors has emerged as a highly sought-after and challenging topic.

articleTitle: Advances in Materials and Junction Engineering Enabled by Epi
abstract: Epitaxy is a powerful technique used in the construction of semiconductor devices, where a monocrystalline film is grown on a surface or structure to create a perfect foundation layer. This technique is used for several purposes, including the deposition of crystalline films with controlled electrical properties, modification of mechanical attributes, and formation of precise junctions with low defect levels. In this paper, we will explore how material and junction engineering can be achieved using epitaxy.

articleTitle: A Novel Method to Improve CMP Selectivity by Ultra-High-Dose Ion Implantation
abstract: The selectivity of Chemical Mechanical Polishing (CMP) is successfully enhanced due to the modification of the film surface by ultra-high-dose ion implantation for the first time. The removal rate of CMP for SiO2 and Si3N4 films was changed by implanted ions. On the contrary, polycrystalline Si (Poly-Si) films had no change regardless of ion implantation. Since C+ is implanted with 3×10<sup>16</sup> ions/cm<sup>2</sup> to SiO2, the removal rate decreases by about 30% lower than that for none doped SiO2 film. However, no significant change was observed after the implantation of C+ at 1×10<sup>16</sup> ions/cm<sup>2</sup> or Si+ to SiO2 and poly films. Furthermore, analyses of film properties by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) load new findings on the chemical reaction between films and slurry.

articleTitle: Advanced contacts on 3D nanostructured channels for vertical transport gate-all-around transistors
abstract: Gate-all-around (GAA) transistors are anticipated to have a substantial impact in achieving logic scaling in the nanometer technology node range, serving as a substitute for the current FinFET technology which lacks acceptable immunity against short channel effect at such miniaturization. GAA transistors offer several advantages over older transistor designs, such as better performance, lower leakage, and reduced energy consumption. This makes them a more sustainable and environmentally friendly alternative to current architectures. In term of integration, vertical gate-all-around devices offer extreme density capability, surpassing equivalent planar technologies. Nevertheless, the development of vertical technology requires rethinking the entire development chain from design to technology. Here, we will present an overview of this technology with a particular focus on the engineering of 3D nanostructured channels and on the integration of S/D contacts on such vertical channels.

articleTitle: Overview of Pixel Scaling Technology in CMOS Image Sensor
abstract: In recent years, the evolution of image sensor has accelerated the combination of imaging and general sensing by leveraging artificial intelligence, making image sensors key devices that support everyday life worldwide [1]. Advanced imaging and sensing technologies should also enhance the quality of life. For instance, imaging technology can elicit human emotions through beautiful images. Sensing technology is expected to find new applications, in areas such as mobility, smart factories, and smart cities. Pixel scaling technology and stacked device integration are driving the market of mobile imaging. The evolution of stack integration can enable new applications while increasing the scalability and flexibility of process technology. Additionally, breakthroughs have been achieved in practical applications of sensing technologies such as depth sensing, event-based vision sensing, and invisible light sensing. The use of image sensors is also increasing to support safe and comfortable living.

articleTitle: Novel Scanning Nanosecond Laser Anneal with Variable Dwell and Real-time Process Control for Advanced Logic and Memory Applications
abstract: As CMOS device scaling continues beyond 5/3 nm nodes, and new device architectures (3D-devices) emerge, the thermal budget requirements have become more stringent. Thermal budget trends, favoring high temperatures at very short time durations to enable high dopant activation and minimize dopant diffusion, have only been accelerating. It is well known that millisecond (msec) Laser Spike Anneal (LSA) improves dopant activation with minimal diffusion. Nanosecond laser anneal in the melt regime could enable further progress through dopant super-activation above the solid solubility limit while practically eliminating dopant diffusion in the solid phase.

articleTitle: The Detailed Analysis of Diffusion Behavior of implanted ions in 4H-SiC
abstract: We studied the diffusion behavior of implanted N, Al, P and Ge into 4H-SiC in detail. The anomalous diffusion of Al and Ge was observed in the case of high dose implantation at room temperature. On the other hand, the slight diffusion was seen at high temperature implantation. These differences would be attributed to the amount of implantation damage. Although the amount of implant damage is almost the same for Al and P, the diffusion of P is small at room temperature implantation. This would be due to the fast recovery rate of implant damage for P. The small diffusion of N can be explained by the small amount of damage due to small mass. The anomalous diffusion of Al is suppressed as decreasing the implantation dose. From these results, it is clear that the implantation damage enhances the diffusion.

articleTitle: Effects of Long-Term Low-Temperature Annealing on Lightly Mg-Implanted GaN
abstract: The excellent properties of GaN are suitable for high-efficiency high-power devices. Especially, excellent high-power GaN MOSFETs are expected to be realized. For this purpose, the ion implantation technology should be established. However, formation of p-type GaN (p-GaN) by ion implantation is still challenging. Recently, Mg-ion implantation has been reported to form p-GaN [1 –5]. Still, post-implantation annealing at a very high temperature is necessary for achieving a high activation rate. By investigating the annealing behavior of defect states electrically, a clue to lower the annealing temperature for activating Mg acceptors might be found. However, a heavy implantation results in a high resistance of GaN layer, which makes the electrical measurements difficult. We investigated the effects of low-temperature annealing on the behavior of defects in lightly Mg-implanted GaN.

articleTitle: Hydrogen Termination Effect on SiO2/Si Interface State Defects of Silicon Hydride and Hydrocarbon Hybrid-Molecular-Ion-Implanted Silicon Epitaxial Wafer
abstract: In recent years, a three-dimensional stacked CMOS image sensor (3D-CIS) has been adopted for high performance. In 3D-CIS, the pixel and the pixel data processing function are fabricated on separate wafers, and the wafers are bonded by Cu-Cu hybrid bonding or Cu through-silicon via (Cu TSV) [1–3].However, it may cause Cu contamination if the barrier layer in the Cuinter connect is insufficient. In addition, deep trench isolation (DTI) isused in the isolation region with the aim of reducing cross talk (mixed colors) with adjacent pixels. In particular, the SiO<inf>2</inf>/Si interface state forms a deep energy level in the silicon band gap and functions as a generation-recombination center (G-R center) of carriers. Since it is well known that this G-R center greatly affects the electrical characteristics of CMOS image sensors, the reduction of interface state density (D<inf>it</inf>) atSiO<inf>2</inf>/Si is an important technical issue [4–10].

articleTitle: Two-Stage Shrinkage Behavior of Multielement-Molecular-Ion-Implantation-Induced Dislocation Loops Revealed by Real-Time TEM Observation
abstract: Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor image sensors (CISs) have important functions in sensing devices in automotive, infrastructural, industrial, and medical applications. One of the most serious technical issues for complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor image sensors (CISs) is dark current originating from pixels. The representative origins of dark current are metal and oxygen impurities, and silicon dioxide (SiO$_{2})/$silicon (Si) interface state defects. Therefore, it is indispensable for high-performance CISs to develop technologies for removal of metal and oxygen impurities from pixels, and reduction of SiO$_{2}/$Si interface state defect density. Recently, we have developed hydrocarbon-molecular-ion $(C_{3} H_{5}$ ion)-implanted epitaxial silicon (Si) wafer as a functional wafer for CISs [1]. In $C_{3} H_{5} -$ion-implanted epitaxial Si wafer, C-interstitial Si precipitates act as gettering sinks [1]. $C_{3} H_{5} -$ion-implanted epitaxial Si wafer can reduce dark current in typical CISs with four-transistor-type pinned photodiode [1] owing to two attractive features of C-interstitial Si precipitates; one is the gettering of metal and oxygen (O) impurities [2], [3], and the another is the trapping of hydrogen (H) [4] and the reduction in SiO$_{2}/$Si interface state defect density by re-release of once-trapped hydrogen [5].

articleTitle: Junction Technology on SiC Power Devices
abstract: Silicon Carbide (SiC) is a very attractive semiconductor material because both n-type and p-type doping control is possible like as Si. However, it must be noted that the diffusivity of the dopants in SiC crystal is extremely low. In Si crystal, the diffusivity of the typical dopants is around 10<sup>-11</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/s at the temperature of 1,200 to 1,300 °C, while in SiC crystal, even boron atom with highest diffusivity among dopant candidates has the value of 10<sup>-14</sup> cm<sup>2</sup>/s even though at the quite high temperature of 1,700 °C [1]. The diffusivity of the donors as phosphorus and nitrogen are four to five orders of magnitude lower than that of boron [2]. Due to such small diffusivity of the dopants, selective area doping technique by the diffusion cannot be applied in SiC. Consequently, ion implantation technique is the only possible way for selective area doping in SiC.

articleTitle: Modulating Electron Energy Barrier at Metal/Semiconductor and Metal/Insulator Contacts with Thin Interfacial Layer
abstract: The electron energy barrier at metal/semiconductor and metal/insulator contacts is one of the crucial elements determining the operational characteristics of electronic and optoelectronic devices. A metal/semiconductor contact is the gateway of charge carrier transport into and out of the active area in all semiconductor devices including Schottky diodes, PN diodes, Bipolar transistors, and field effect transistors. The charge carrier transport through the contact, regulated mainly by the interface energy barrier, is directly tied to the functionality of device such as rectification and its power consumption manifesting the contact resistance. A metal/insulator contact takes part in constructing the metal/oxide/semiconductor (MOS) structure adopted in MOS capacitor and MOS field effect transistor (MOSFET). In this case, the interface energy barrier makes a dominant influence on the threshold voltage at which the inversion channel is induced on the semiconductor side.

articleTitle: Ion implantation-induced damage in 4H-SiC detected by photo-modulated reflectance
abstract: The benefits of the wide bandgap semiconductor silicon carbide (SiC) for use in high-voltage and low-loss power devices [1] are driven by fundamental material properties of high breakdown field and thermal conductivity. Ion implantation is a key doping technique in SiC device processing which requires efficient methods for dose monitoring after room temperature or elevated temperature implantation. In this work we apply photo-modulated reflectance (PMR) as an effective technique to monitor implantation dose and implantation temperature through electro-optic and thermo-optic effects influenced by residual defects in as-implanted SiC. Note, the PMR technique is widely used for implantation process monitoring in silicon device manufacturing. The present work on 4H-SiC is based on our previous experience with the PMR technique applied for Si wafers implanted with different dopants in a wide range of ion energies and ion doses [2 –4].

articleTitle: Development of p-type Ion Implantation Technique for Realization of GaN Vertical MOSFETs
abstract: GaN has attracted attention as a semiconductor material for next-generation power switching devices. Vertical-type GaN devices with MOS gate driving are preferable for high-power switching applications. Due to recent advances in bulk GaN crystal growth [1], more studies are reporting vertical-type GaN devices with a breakdown voltage exceeding 1 kV on GaN substrates [2, 3]. However, these reports use an epitaxially grown p-type layer or fin-structure.

articleTitle: Room-Temperature Atomic Layer Deposition: a Review
abstract: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) has become an indispensable technology for the production of ultra-large-scale integration, since it allows for metal oxide stacking with an atomic-level thickness precision [1]. In the ALD process, the metal-oxide deposition takes place by repeating the metal organic (MO) gas saturation followed by the its reactivation with the oxidizing gas [1]. The saturation and reactivation were separated with the vacuum pumping or the inert gas purging. Since it utilizes the gas saturation mechanism, the conformal deposition on the complicated surface is possible. In the conventional ALD, the reactivation was performed with an introduction of oxidizing gas and zone heating around 300 °C although the suppression of the process temperature to room temperature (RT) was demanded for the flexible electronics and micromachines. In our laboratory, on the other hand, we confirmed that the OH radicals produced from the plasma excited humidified Ar effectively oxidizes the metal organic saturation layer at RT [2]. Since then, the RT-ALD has been developed with the OH radicals for depositions of various kinds of metal oxides [2–11]. In this paper, the schematic of the RT-ALD system and the related experimental results are explained as a review. The application to the electronic devices is also explained here.

articleTitle: EZ-FET junctions activation by nanosecond laser annealing
abstract: The EZ-FET (easy-FET) is a simple FDSOI-like (Fully Depleted Silicon On Insulator) device that can be used for the electrical characterization of Si layers fabricated with various types of approaches. It notably enables to assess and benchmark Si layers fabricated with a low thermal budget, for instance for 3D sequential integration [1]. For an efficient characterization of Low Temperature (LT) films, the full EZ-FET integration should be processed at low temperature, including the gate stack deposition and dopants activation for junctions formation. To get past the limitations of LT dopants activation, we proposed in [2] a junctionless EZ-FET that can be used for the extraction of thin film parameters. However, due to its access resistance limitations, it does not allow an accurate extraction of front-channel parameters.

articleTitle: Ion Implantation Doping Technology for Ga2O3 and Its Application to Device Fabrication
abstract: Gallium oxide (Ga<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf>) has attracted great attention as a next-generation power electronics material because of its extremely large bandgap energy of 4.5 eV and the existence of high-quality single-crystal substrates that can be manufactured from melt-grown bulks [1 –4]. Although it is not well known, Ga<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> possesses excellent applicability of ion implantation doping processes unlike conventional compound semiconductors.

articleTitle: Doping of silicon by phosphorus end-terminated polymers: shallow junction formation by thermal and laser annealing
abstract: Alternative approaches for doping of silicon have been the subject of an intense research activity to overcome the limitations of conventional doping techniques when applied to non-planar devices [1–4]. Recently, polymers terminated with a dopant containing moiety have been proposed as a viable solution for the doping of the new evolving 3D nanostructures [5]. The self-limiting nature of the grafting process of these molecules onto not deglazed Si surfaces has been widely investigated over the past few years, demonstrating the possibility to effectively control the concentration of P atoms on the sample surface [5, 6]. Additionally, high activation rate values (η<inf>a</inf> > 80%) were reported for this specific system upon drive-in of P atoms by conventional thermal treatments at high temperature in a standard RTP machine [7]. In this work, the possibility to combine this alternative doping technology with pulsed laser melting (PLM) is investigated, demonstrating the effective capability to form abrupt phosphorus junctions in silicon substrates.

articleTitle: Effects of Ion Channeling and Co-implants on Ion Ranges and Damage in Si: Studies with PL, SRP, SIMS and MC models
abstract: This study uses photoluminescence (PL) and other carrier-recombination sensitive probes in combination with spreading resistance profiling (SRP), SIMS and IMSIL MC-calculations to monitor the ion range and damage levels in highly-channeled and random beam orientation 7.5 MeV B and 10 MeV P and As profiles and various combinations of co-implants with 50 keV Phosphorus implants in Silicon(100). The effects of annealing on the 10 MeV profiles showed the strong shifts in PL data from implant damage in the as-implanted and annealed samples. Curious “intermittencies” were seen in the PL signals from MeV implant defect centers.

articleTitle: History of junction technologies Commemorative talk for the 75th anniversary of the transistor
abstract: In this paper, I describe the history of junction technologies for ICT (Information and Communication Technology) devices. Junctions serve as functional interfaces between materials in these devices. Over the past200 years, since the inception of electrical engineering, a wide range of junction technologies have been developed as key components for device operation, playing a significant role in advancing intelligence in human society.
